channel.title: Muhammad Jahanzaib Awan — Writing
channel.description: Short technical posts on machine learning, evaluation and data science.

item.title: Cold Start Problems: What to Do With No Data Yet
item.description: No historical data, no labels, no user behaviour yet. Here is a practical way to reason about cold starts without pretending you have data you don't.

item.title: A/B Testing ML Models in Production, Done Properly
item.description: Offline AUC improvements often vanish or backfire online. Here is how to run an A/B test for a production ML model that you can actually trust.

item.title: What a Validation Curve Tells You Before the Test Set
item.description: The shape of a validation curve, not just its final number, tells you whether to add capacity, add data, or stop tuning entirely.

item.title: Choosing a Loss Function: Matching Maths to the Problem
item.description: Your loss function encodes what counts as a mistake. Pick one that doesn't match the real cost of errors, and your model will optimise for the wrong thing quietly.

item.title: How to Benchmark a Computer Vision Model Honestly
item.description: A practical guide to leakage-aware splits, strong baselines, and realistic test conditions before shipping a vision model.

item.title: Data Versioning for ML: Why Git Alone Falls Short
item.description: Git tracks your code perfectly and your data terribly. Here is why that mismatch causes silent, hard-to-debug failures in ML pipelines.

item.title: Feature Importance Methods: What They Tell You
item.description: Feature importance scores describe a model's behaviour, not the world. Knowing the difference stops you from overtrusting a bar chart.

item.title: Ensemble Methods Explained Without the Jargon
item.description: A plain-English guide to bagging, boosting, and stacking, with a concrete example showing why each one actually works.

item.title: Building Your First End to End ML Project That Actually Ships
item.description: Most first ML projects die from scope, not skill. Here is how to size one so it actually finishes and teaches you something true.

item.title: The Maths You Actually Need Before a Deep Learning Book
item.description: Skip the full maths degree. Here is the small, specific set of ideas that makes deep learning books click, with a worked example.

item.title: Reading a Machine Learning Job Advert Properly
item.description: Machine learning job ads are full of vague phrases like 'strong background in deep learning'. Here is what they usually mean in practice.

item.title: How to Choose a Machine Learning Course That Is Worth It
item.description: Most ML courses look similar on paper. The ones worth your money teach evaluation rigour, not just model zoos.

item.title: What Deep Learning Adds That Classical ML Cannot
item.description: Deep learning's real edge is automatic representation learning, not magic accuracy. Here is when that matters and when it does not.

item.title: RMSE, MAE, and When Each One Lies to You
item.description: RMSE and MAE often disagree about which model is best. Here is the intuition behind why, with a worked example you can check by hand.

item.title: Choosing a Segmentation Metric: Why Accuracy Lies
item.description: Pixel accuracy flatters lazy segmentation models. Dice, IoU and boundary metrics tell you what accuracy hides.

item.title: Data Labelling for Vision: Annotation Quality Sets Your Ceiling
item.description: Better models cannot outrun bad labels. A close look at how annotation ambiguity, guideline drift, and inter-annotator disagreement cap what any vision model can learn.

item.title: Video Understanding vs Image Classification: The Extra Axis
item.description: Time is not just another axis. It breaks independence assumptions, inflates apparent accuracy, and demands leakage-aware splits that most video pipelines quietly skip.

item.title: Optical Character Recognition: From Pipelines to Deep Nets
item.description: A tour through classical OCR pipelines and the specific failure modes that end-to-end deep learning actually solved, not just automated.

item.title: Anomaly Detection in Vision: One-Class Methods Made Simple
item.description: Most defects are rare and unlabelled. One-class methods learn what normal looks like, then flag anything that does not fit, no anomaly examples required.

item.title: Convolutional Networks Versus Vision Transformers, Honestly
item.description: CNNs and ViTs both work well on images, but they fail differently under small data and distribution shift. I compare them with a concrete worked example.
